title: Reading the Grass
passage:
Nothing is sown in bands and nothing is cut to two heights. The stripes that make a well-kept pitch look like a length of corduroy are laid after the blade has passed, by the heavy roller behind it: grass pressed away from you throws the light back and reads as pale, grass pressed towards you swallows it and reads as dark. Which is why, as the groundsman Elis Torvund likes to tell visiting apprentices, the same pitch is never quite the same pitch twice. Walk round to the opposite stand at half-time and every pale band has gone dark and every dark band pale, though not a blade has moved. A camera slung high above the halfway line sees a third version again, and a spectator down at pitch level, looking along the rows rather than across them, may find almost no pattern there at all. The pattern is not in the grass. It is in the angle you happen to be standing at.
— Marit Lundh, sports notebook

questions.prompt: According to the text, why does a striped pitch look different when viewed from the far stand rather than the near one?

options.text: Because the bands come from the way the grass is lying, the same rows are read the other way round from the far side.
Because the roller leaves the grass leaning towards one end of the ground, the far half of a pitch always looks darker than the near half.
Because floodlights and low afternoon sun reach the two ends of a ground at different angles and alter the colour of the grass.
Because the rows are cut to two slightly different heights, and the shorter rows show more of the dark soil beneath them from some seats.

questions.rationale: TYPE-001 direct detail, joining the mechanism sentence to the observation sentence. The text pins the effect on the direction the grass has been pressed — 'grass pressed away from you throws the light back and reads as pale, grass pressed towards you swallows it and reads as dark' — and then reports that from the opposite stand 'every pale band has gone dark and every dark band pale, though not a blade has moved'; A paraphrases that swap and its cause. B = wrong mechanism with a quantifier upgrade: the roller is real in the text, but it lays alternating rows rather than tipping the whole sward one way, and the passage describes bands swapping, not one half of the ground being permanently darker. C = outside_knowledge: lighting angle is a plausible real-world cause of colour differences, but the text attributes nothing to floodlights or sun and states explicitly that the grass itself has not changed. D = contradiction: the opening sentence rules it out — 'nothing is cut to two heights' — and no soil is mentioned anywhere.

generator_meta.topic: why stadium grass is mowed in stripes — the pattern is an optical effect of which way the roller has laid the grass relative to the viewer, not a difference in the grass itself
